Unless Valve takes some serious steps to curb the onslaught of AI-created games on its store (and right now you cannot even filter new release lists to remove games with AI declarations), I find it hard to believe we’ll see fewer than 30,000 games released on Steam in 2027, possibly far more. text:
According to SteamDB, a total of 21,248 new games were added to Valve’s PC store in 2025. That was almost 3,000 more than 2024, which itself beat 2023 by over 4,000. 2026 is going to smash that record again, and we know this because it already has, and it’s only mid-October. But this could be nothing compared to what we’ll see in 2027.

As spotted by Bredan Keogh on BlueSky, today marks the moment that Steam releases during 2026 exceeded those from all of 2025. We’re now at a total of 21,388, with two-and-a-half months of the year—traditionally the busiest ones for game releases—still remaining. SteamPageAnalyzer is projecting that the total will reach at least 24,000.

This is, obviously, a silly number of games. It breaks down to 66 games releasing each day, up from 55 in 2025, creating a market that’s ever more cluttered and in which a growing number of extremely good games will drown. This sucks, but thankfully is something Steam owner Valve is slowly working on, with recent ideas like the prominent front-page spot for Your Personal Calendar. This is a ten-box section of games the Steam algo suspects you’ll be interested in playing, whether because you’ve previously wishlisted them, or because they match the sorts of games you tend to play, and it’s pretty good at doing it. Some developers are also anecdotally reporting that it’s helping their games get seen by the people more likely to buy them, and hopefully Valve will lean in and continue to innovate in these areas. Except, this could be about to get a whole lot harder.

Vibe-coded game, are springing up increasingly frequently, and with recent changes to Claude allowing the quick and easy decompilation of other developers’ games, it’s already starting to get much worse.

Back in July, Nicole Carpenter reported on the growing power of vibe coding, explaining how it made creating rip-offs of existing games something that takes only a matter of hours. And this month it became far, far more common thanks to Anthropic’s latest Claude Opus 5.5, leading to web-based versions of established games springing up faster than they can be taken down, and worse, being extremely good at the process.

Given Steam has long been home to avalanches of the latest form of low-grade gaming crap, whether it’s achievement-farming idle games, “desktop companion games,” or whatever the slop du jour might be, it’s now victim to the inescapable lava flow of vibe-coded guff. So just imagine where things will be in 2027.

The one limitation to getting a game on Steam, beyond the spurious verification processes, is a $100 charge. This nominal fee, intended to try to put off chancers who intend to release a barely-functioning asset flip from bothering, is clearly failing in its role, and with vibe-coded knock-offs likely to become the norm, such games will only become actually better to play, and thus more likely to make some money.

Unless Valve takes some serious steps to curb the onslaught of AI-created games on its store (and right now you cannot even filter new release lists to remove games with AI declarations), I find it hard to believe we’ll see fewer than 30,000 games released on Steam in 2027, possibly far more. No matter how much algorithm-driven curation there might be, it’ll only get harder for an unknown but great game to find its way to the surface amidst such carnage.
